title: Customs Legislation Amendment (False Trade Marks Infringement Notices) Bill 2026
short_title: Customs Legislation Amendment (False Trade Marks Infringement Notices) Bill 2026

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would create an offence for importing goods bearing false trade marks and let the Australian Border Force issue infringement notices instead of prosecuting.
Infringement notices could impose penalties of up to 15 penalty units on individuals or 75 penalty units on companies under the existing customs scheme.
The changes would cover imports after commencement, set by proclamation or automatically after six months following Royal Assent, and would complement existing seizure arrangements.
changes: The new strict liability offence would carry maximum court fines of 60 penalty units for individuals and 300 for companies.
A defence would cover marks applied or altered with permission from the registered owner or an authorised user.
The new offence would be inserted into Schedule 8 to the Customs Regulation so that infringement notices become available for it.
summary.affected: Importers, registered trade mark owners, authorised users and Australian Border Force officers are affected.

speeches.speaker: Julian Hill
speeches.brief: Moved that the Customs Legislation Amendment (False Trade Marks Infringement Notices) Bill 2026 be read a second time, proposing a strict liability offence and infringement notices for importing counterfeit goods, particularly commercial quantities of high-risk consumer products, to strengthen deterrence and protect consumers and Australian businesses.

speeches.speaker: Tony Burke
speeches.brief: Declared that the Customs Legislation Amendment (False Trade Marks Infringement Notices) Bill 2026 and Treasury Laws Amendment (Delivering an Efficient and Trusted Tax System) Bill 2026 stood referred to the Federation Chamber for further consideration.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Hastie
speeches.brief: Argued that the Customs Legislation Amendment (False Trade Marks Infringement Notices) Bill 2026 addresses counterfeit imports through a strict liability offence, financial penalties and Australian Border Force infringement powers, but raised concerns about proportionality, consultation and the absence of a clear trigger, and supported referral to a Senate inquiry.

speeches.speaker: Rowan Holzberger
speeches.brief: Supported the Customs Legislation Amendment (False Trade Marks Infringement Notices) Bill 2026, arguing it would ease the burden on businesses and protect consumers from dangerous counterfeit goods, including medical devices, toys and chainsaws; the bill was read a second time and ordered to be reported without amendment.

speeches.speaker: Lisa Darmanin
speeches.brief: Presented the fifth report of 2026 of the Selection of Bills Committee, recommending referrals of specified bills to parliamentary committees for inquiry and reporting by 30 April 2026, 5 May 2026, or 19 June 2026. Moved that the report be adopted, and the question was agreed to.

speeches.speaker: Anthony Chisholm
speeches.brief: Moved the second reading of a bill creating a strict liability offence for importing goods with false trade marks and enabling infringement notices. The measure responds to over 700,000 counterfeit items seized in the 2024-25 financial year, supports enforcement by the Australian Border Force and aims to protect consumers and legitimate businesses.

speeches.speaker: Katy Gallagher
speeches.brief: Moved that government business, including five specified bills and a related bill subject to introduction, be considered from 12.15 pm until no later than 1.30 pm, followed by general business notice of motion no. 510 concerning the 2026-27 Budget. The question was agreed to.

speeches.speaker: Susan McDonald
speeches.brief: Argued that the bill would create a strict liability offence for importing goods with false trademarks and allow Australian Border Force to issue infringement notices. Supported action against counterfeit goods but raised concerns about proportionality, personal imports, limited consultation and safeguards; the bill was ultimately supported and read a second time.
